final_answer:
Bottom line: The husband's best (and effectively only practical) route is a motion to reopen and rescind the in absentia removal order filed with the immigration court (the Immigration Judge who entered the order) under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii), 8 U.S.C. 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii), and 8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii), on the ground that he did not receive notice under INA 239(a)(1) or (2). Once the order is rescinded, the denial of his adjustment application can be cured before the court; the I-130 must be separately revived with USCIS.

1. What to file with the immigration court. A written motion to rescind the August 1, 2025 in absentia order and reopen proceedings (filed with the Immigration Court having administrative control of the record, with proof of service on DHS/ICE OPLA; e-filing via ECAS where available). Request that the motion expressly invoke 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) (lack of notice) and not merely general reopening. Attach: (a) the husband's sworn declaration (and the wife's) that they never received the NTA, hearing notice or the RFE, never provided the address used, lived at/used the address they gave USCIS on the I-130/I-485, and only learned of the order on April 1, 2026; (b) copies of the I-130/I-485 showing the address actually provided, any change-of-address (AR-11) records, the USCIS denial notices and mailing envelopes/notices showing the wrong address; (c) the NTA and any hearing notice (obtain via EOIR automated case information, a FOIA/ROP request, or the court) showing the address used; (d) evidence of diligence (prompt filing, case-status checks) ; and (e) a proposed order. Also include the Form EOIR-33 change of address if not already filed, and Form EOIR-28 if represented. Because relief is sought on lack of notice, there is no time limit ('at any time') and the filing of the motion automatically stays removal pending the IJ's decision (8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii); INA 240(b)(5)(C)). Only one such motion is allowed. Consider alternatively and in the same filing pleading, as a fallback, ordinary reopening (180-day deadline for exceptional circumstances has long expired; sua sponte reopening is discretionary) - but lack of notice is the strong ground. Note: if the husband would be seeking ordinary (non-notice) reopening, the fee would apply; a lack-of-notice motion is distinct.

2. Fees. As of April 1, 2026: no EOIR filing fee for a motion to reopen an in absentia order filed under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) on lack of notice. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (July 4, 2025) imposed a motion-to-reopen/reconsider fee (originally $900; inflation-adjusted for FY2026, with sources suggesting about $1,045 for a later period), but expressly excepts in absentia motions under 240(b)(5)(C)(ii); EOIR regs (8 CFR 1003.24(b)(2)(iii), 1003.8(a)(2)) carry the exemption. If the motion were also (or instead) framed as ordinary reopening, the OBBBA fee would apply; I could not retrieve the primary fee schedule text directly (government sites were blocked), so the exact current dollar figure is secondary-source based and unverified. Fee waivers are generally restricted under OBBBA. Separate: if reopened and the husband renews adjustment before the IJ, a USCIS Form I-485 filing fee may be required (to be paid to DHS, not EOIR) - verify current fee guidance; not verified here.

3. Contesting the I-485 denial. USCIS I-485 denials are not appealable, but 8 CFR 1245.2(a)(5)(ii) lets an applicant renew an adjustment application before an IJ after USCIS denial once removal proceedings exist (and the IJ has exclusive jurisdiction under 1245.2(a)(1)(i)). So after rescission, the husband can renew adjustment before the IJ. As an immediate relative of a US citizen who was inspected and admitted (B-2), INA 245(a) is available and the 245(c) bars (e.g., unauthorized employment, status violations) do not apply to immediate relatives (INA 245(c)); the overstay is not a bar. Marriage after entry (December 20, 2022) is not a misrepresentation presumption problem for immediate relatives in the same way as 90-day rule matters only for 212(a)(6)(C) fraud analysis (the marriage came 19 days after entry; DOS 90-day rule is a visa-adjudication guideline; assess preconceived-intent risk). Bona fides must be proven.

4. Contesting the I-130 denial. IJs have no jurisdiction over I-130 petitions. The I-130 denial (December 5, 2023) was appealable to the BIA within 30 days and a USCIS motion to reopen/reconsider under 8 CFR 103.5(a) is due within 30 days (33 if mailed) - both expired. Options: (i) file a new I-130 (with fee, with full RFE-responsive evidence) and ask the IJ to continue/administratively close proceedings or (post-2025 policy dependent) for USCIS adjudication; (ii) file a late 103.5 motion with USCIS arguing the failure to respond was due to USCIS's own misdirected RFE (USCIS may excuse delay where reasonable and beyond control for motions to reopen - 103.5(a)(1)(i)); relief is discretionary; (iii) request USCIS correction of agency error, congressional/ombudsman inquiry. A new I-130 filed while in proceedings is permitted. Also the wife may file a new I-130 with a new bona fides package. Note that USCIS denial for abandonment/non-response rather than merits means no merits finding precluding refiling.

5. Risks/counterpoints. Under Campos-Chaves v. Garland, 602 U.S. 447 (2024), a defective NTA (missing time/place) is not itself a basis to rescind if a proper hearing notice was received - the movant must show he lacked notice under either 239(a)(1) or (2). Here the claim is stronger: both documents were mailed to an address he never provided. Under Matter of G-Y-R-, 23 I&N Dec. 181 (BIA 2002), and Matter of M-D-, 23 I&N Dec. 540 (BIA 2002), mailing to the last address the respondent provided creates a presumption of delivery; if the address used was not one he provided under 239(a)(1)(F), constructive notice does not arise and the presumption does not apply. DHS may argue he provided or could be charged with the address (verify the NTA address source) and that he failed to keep the court informed; he must show he never was served with an NTA containing address-obligation warnings. Also, a newer BIA decision (30 I&N Dec. 1 (BIA 2026)) appeared in search results and I did not read it; it should be checked. Also, given no showing that he provided any address to the court, DHS may argue USCIS-address issues are irrelevant; he should show the correct address was on file with USCIS. If the IJ denies, appeal to the BIA within 30 days (EOIR-26, fee) and petition for review within 30 days to the court of appeals (INA 242). Practical concern: prompt filing is advisable given current enforcement; the automatic stay applies upon filing.

authorities.title: Rescission of in absentia order

authorities.proposition: Lack-of-notice motion may be filed any time; one motion; automatic stay

Notice defense is strong because address was never provided by respondent; Campos-Chaves requires lack of notice under both paragraphs
